title: Chapter 15: PART 15 - The Morning We Kept Our Names 114

author: admin

blocks.text: I stepped close enough for the candlelight to shine through the veil and threw the gathered silk across Claudia’s knife hand.
Eleanor drove her elbow backward and dropped her weight at the same instant.
The knife turned outward through the silk.
Then the captain was there, forcing her arm away from Eleanor while a guard seized her other shoulder.
My burned hand struck the wood hard enough to send pain up my arm, but the veil stayed wrapped around the knife until the captain took it from me.
Eleanor stumbled into the prince’s arms.
The physician reached her before I could stand straight.
I watched him press a clean cloth beneath her jaw.
For a moment nobody said anything that I could understand.
Mother lowered herself beside me on the cathedral floor and put her arms around me as though I were still sixteen and the world had only just frightened me.
Across the marble, Claudia struggled once against the guards.
The king ordered her removed to a guarded chamber beyond the cathedral, and this time the order went through the doors without being altered by anyone on its way.
Lady Arden stood apart from Eleanor until her daughter looked toward her.
Eleanor held the physician’s cloth against her throat.
For once she did not ask someone else to make the answer easier.
Eleanor sat, then reached for her companion’s hand, and the prince knelt beside them both.
The archbishop closed the marriage register without adding a single vow.
I watched him record the attempted burning, the threat with the knife, and the names of everyone who had seen them.
Mother’s confinement went into the same record.
So did the king’s authorization and the prince’s signature.
The truth was not made smaller to spare the people who had been powerful enough to overlook it.
In the weeks that followed, the old estate records were gathered from Bellamont and the Arden properties.
Mother’s stitch record directed the examiners to the altered authorization, and the surviving account books supplied what memory alone could not.
Household officers had accepted money for obedience.
The keeper confessed fully once he understood that silence would no longer protect him.
Claudia’s confession papers were examined beside the evidence of the threats used to obtain them, and neither Mother nor Alice was punished for the crimes they had been forced to claim.
The formal judgment against Claudia named the fraud, the unlawful confinements, the conspiracy to deceive the crown, and the attack everyone in the cathedral had witnessed.
She lost her authority, her household, and the freedom she had taken from other women so easily.
Lady Arden faced judgment for the petitions she had signed and the confinement she had helped conceal.
Love, she told her mother, could not require pretending that harm had never happened.
The king ordered the surviving blank authorizations canceled and replaced the practice that had allowed completed instructions to hide above old signatures.
He acknowledged that in front of the court when her name was formally cleared.
I stood beside her while the correction to the household register was read aloud.
Mother listened without crying until the clerk reached the line restoring her wages.
It was such a small dream that I nearly broke beneath it.
We took rooms with windows low enough to see the street.
For several nights she slept with the door open, and I left a lamp burning where she could see it from her bed.
Some mornings she woke before dawn and touched the latch.
Some evenings she asked whether I had truly come home.
I learned to answer without making her ashamed of the question.
I left my place among the waiting women and accepted paid work helping preserve the palace’s damaged textiles, with written terms that Mother insisted on reading twice.
On days when her hands hurt, she sat by the window and watched people pass.
Months later, Eleanor and the prince returned to the cathedral of Bellamont.
Their settlement had been read aloud in advance.
Their signatures had been witnessed separately.
Eleanor retained the authority over her house that Claudia had tried to steal.
Lady Arden sat in the front pew, and Eleanor greeted her with affection that carried boundaries neither woman pretended were temporary.
Mother and I sat together among the invited guests.
The original veil had been preserved with the evidence, its burned border left visible so nobody could mistake beauty for innocence again.
For the wedding, Mother had embroidered a new one.
Eleanor lifted it herself before the prince spoke.
When the vows were finished, Mother slipped her hand into mine, and I felt the familiar bend of her smallest finger against my palm.
For eight years I had believed she had chosen a life without me.
Now the cathedral doors stood open, sunlight lay across the marble, and when we walked out together, no one had the power to tell either of us to disappear.
